stadtsimulation.inhalt:
\\ Spatial Processes

Urban Simulation
Simulation and Visualization of the Dynamics of Spatial Processes in Cities

Reinhard KÖNIG

Dipl. Ing. Reinhard König, Chair of Urban District Planning and Design, TU Karlsruhe,  

1. INTRODUCTION

Urban structures result from various continuously running, mutually interacting processes. If one depicts the appearance of a city at a particular moment, one obtains merely a snapshot of this dynamic system. The aim of the project described below is to represent the city as a continuous process.

The field of spatial planning encompasses the organization of spatial structures and their interactions with social processes. Planning always means the conceptual anticipation of states that do not yet exist. Current planning practice, however, concentrates merely on comparing the target state with the actual state. Essential for sustainable urban development, though, would be an engagement with the processes that have led, or are intended to lead, to the respective states. Both a thorough analysis of the relationships relevant to urban development and a conscious handling of the dynamics and temporal properties of processes have remained alien to spatial planning. Accordingly, plans are still static representations, while plans in the form of dynamic maps are unknown.

To visualize spatial processes, urban dynamics must first be simulated in space and time. The basis of this simulation is a 'bottom-up' description of urban processes by means of mathematical models, which in a further step are translated into algorithms for computer processing. The course of the calculations and the development of the system are to be represented graphically.

2. STATE OF RESEARCH

The formal representation and simulation of a city including all its essential subsystems[1] is referred to in the literature as a 'Large-Scale Urban Model'. The development of such comprehensive urban models began in the USA in the 1950s. The starting point was Johann Heinrich von Thünen's location theory of 1826, which investigated how a spatial equilibrium distribution of settlements, land uses, and population comes about[2].

Building on this work, various fundamental geographical "laws" were discovered, all of which are based on an economic understanding of optimality. Three of these laws are particularly relevant for understanding urban systems: the law of the distribution of central places[3], the law of the allocation of development potential as a function of settlement size[4] , and the law of the equilibrium distribution of land rent, whose level decreases with distance from the city center[5]. Further components such as population, jobs, services, and the transportation system were added and influenced the formation of equilibrium. Also significant is Torsten Hägerstrand's theory of the spatial diffusion of innovations, first published in 1952[6].

The first attempt to combine these components in an "integrated" urban model was made by Lowry[7] in 1964, using the example of Pittsburgh. This model, however, was static and rested on the assumption that a city as a whole is always in a state of equilibrium. To divide the city into sectors among which the activities were allocated, a grid with a resolution of one square mile was assumed. This subdivision already recalls the structure of a cellular automaton.

Jay Forrester[8] was the first to develop an approach for a dynamic urban model, in 1969. In it, positive feedback is described as the main cause of the complex and counterintuitive behavior of natural and, in particular, urban systems. In Forrester's model, one feedback loop always dominates the entire system until it is superseded by another. The computer was an indispensable tool for studying the behavior of this dynamic model. A change in the input parameters resulted in a change of the equilibrium state. This relationship was intuitively comprehensible and linear. The main problem with his model was that it embodied an overly general view of the urban system (based on average values) and lacked any spatial reference (numerical simulation without a graphical interface), which was presumably due to Forrester's disregard of the geographical theory of his time.

Most of the simulations developed to date are based on the basic concepts of Lowry and Forrester and attempt to relate the essential components of a city – housing, work, services, land use, and transportation system – to one another within a single model. For a detailed explanation of how the most recent models work, I refer to M. Wegener's article "Urban Land-Use Transportation Models"[9]. The goal in developing these models was to ensure a balance between understanding of the process, complexity of the description, and availability of data. What all these model conceptions have in common is a reductionist (top-down) perspective, which attempts to study systems by dividing them into logically justified components.

In the following, I would like to concentrate on the criticism of the comprehensive modeling approaches. The most influential and popular attack came from Douglas B. Lee[10] and was published in 1973 under the title "Requiem for Large-Scale Models". It describes 'Seven Sins of Large-Scale Models', which form the core of the criticism and, in modified form, are partly still put forward today.

Lee's list of seven sins begins with 'Hypercomprehensiveness’ (excessive comprehensiveness), the attempt to explain too much with a single model. Concretely, this means that too many variables are coupled into processes whose explanatory power and correctness cannot be verified. Adding further aspects with the intention of completing the model leads, contrary to that intention, to lower accuracy, since more "ignorance" enters into it. Furthermore, 'Wrongheadedness’ (obstinacy) means that, owing to the integration of too many constraints and relationships within the model structure, the resulting mechanisms can no longer be understood or distinguished even by the model's builder. From today's perspective (e.g., with regard to chaos research), it is easy to see that additional variables and relationships make a system increasingly dependent on its initial parameters and that relatively small errors can lead to a completely different and false understanding of the underlying process.

A further problem is identified by the term 'hungriness’ (hunger), which expresses the enormous amount of data required. In combination with 'complicatedness’ (complicatedness), this leads to the charge that model builders are unable to develop an adequate understanding of the 'black box' constructs they themselves have created in complex models. This means that a user has no clue as to how, after a change in an input variable, the corresponding output value comes about[11]. In case of doubt, this problem of traceability leads to a loss of the model's credibility. Moreover, it enables the programmer to adjust the model by setting restrictions so that it delivers the desired results. 'Grossness’ (coarseness) further aggravates the problems, as the models work with "aggregated" data (average values) in order to reduce complicatedness, but thereby, despite the enormous amounts of data, permit only general statements at the global level and not at the local level, where they would be needed for planning decisions.

Besides these points, which remain problematic today, sins are listed that from today's perspective have lost their relevance through technological progress: 'Mechanicalness’, which referred to the computing problems of the time arising from rounding errors or the significance of the sequential processing of a task, as well as from the difficulty of preparing a problem for the computer, 'Expensiveness’ (costliness), which stands for the high costs that had to be incurred for obtaining the required data and forecasts. The municipal and regional geographic information systems (GIS) introduced since the 1980s did cost a fortune, but they are established today and can be used as a data basis for the models.

To deal with the set of problems outlined, the present project draws on findings from systems theory and specifically from the subfield concerned with complex systems, complexity theory, which will be discussed in detail later. It can be stated in advance that the guidelines for model builders that Lee lists at the end of his article, which have meanwhile become generally accepted, agree with the principles of complexity research.

According to Lee, one of the most important criteria of a model is its transparency. It should be easy to understand for every user with reasonable effort. This requirement corresponds to the reduction to the essential system parameters and their relations. This ensures that, in the event of inconsistencies in the model, the persons involved can discover and name them, which in turn makes it possible, after reaching a consensus on the initial assumptions, to agree on the results and to ensure fruitful cooperation among those involved in the planning process.

Furthermore, in conceiving a model, a balance between theory, objectivity, and intuition should be sought. The approach should be guided by the problem at hand and select methods accordingly, not the other way around.

In summary, a model should be kept formally as simple as possible, since complexity arises "automatically" within the model structure.

3. OBJECTIVES

A city is a complex system par excellence. The inhabitants and their dwellings, the shops and production facilities, the movement of goods and people are closely interwoven. There are numerous dynamic dependencies among them, insofar as a change affecting one of the parts can have complex effects on other parts within the overall system.

The central task of the project is to explore the rules of the individual elements that, in their interplay, form through self-organization mechanisms the complex structures we can observe in cities. I assume that certain relationships – each with different weightings – apply to all settlements worldwide[12]. First and foremost, this concerns the economic laws of trade in goods and resources, as well as the behavior of the individual and collective actors in a city, i.e., that of citizens and of political or economic groups. In spatial economics, these relationships are treated as interactions of structure (location theory), interaction (spatial mobility theory), and process (regional growth and development theory)[13].

In the context of complexity theory, within which the research project is developed, the investigations must start from the smallest meaningful elements in order to explain the higher-level emergent phenomena. Accordingly, before dealing with the models of the individual urban components, a simulation concept must be introduced that shows how the urban system can be represented computationally. This concept comprises the general approach as well as the representation of the elements and their interactions. The subsequent methodology will build on this foundation.

The nature of the urban system is explored by first investigating the respective subsystems by means of simple, abstract submodels, whose relationships with one another are intended to explain the questions of the subsystems. In the last phase of the project, the individual subsystems are finally connected with one another, thus forming a dynamic overall system.

The first subsystem deals with the distribution of population in space. Why do the actors settle where they do, with which elements do they interact, and which activity spaces do they claim for themselves?

This is followed by the subsystem of the land market , which is intended to shed light on what leads to the formation of centers in both monocentric and polycentric structures, how urban functions are distributed, and which forces lie behind the processes of sprawl and agglomeration.

A further subsystem is transportation. It is closely linked with the first two subsystems and deals with the influence of the transportation system and transportation technology on the land market and the distribution of population, and vice versa.

After these basic topics have been treated, the project turns to the changes of structures. Why, and according to which pattern (periodic or chaotic), do structures change over time?

Finally, the environment comes into focus. Here it must be clarified what role environmental influences play in urban development and what feedback on the other subsystems results from emissions and immissions.

Finally, it is explained why the visualization of the course of dynamic processes is an important component of the project and which possibilities open up for planning . That is, what strategies for sustainable urban development might look like and how they can be used in the education of urban designers and in the practice of urban design.

4. METHODOLOGY

Complexity and self-organization have already been mentioned repeatedly. At this point, the fundamentals behind these terms will be summarized once more.

The simulation of the city conceived here can be understood as an adaptive collective of interacting units and thus stands in contrast to the 'top-down' approaches of the 'Large-Scale Urban Models' described in the section on the state of research. The present project is characterized by a generative (bottom-up) approach. Phenomena are understood as a product (or synthesis) of multiple interactions of simple elementary units.

Self-organization and emergence are essential for understanding generative systems. The appearance of higher-level (global) phenomena on the basis of a limited number of rules or prescriptions applied at the local level to many abstract entities is called emergence. Such emergent phenomena may be, for example, collective behavior or spatial patterns that seem to organize themselves through the interplay of the individual parts, as the interactions lead to mutual adaptations over time. The essence of self-organization lies in the way in which the interactions among the elements and with the environment take place. John Holland described these relationships with the memorable formula "much coming from little". Examples of such phenomena can be found in traffic jams, urban slums, or ethnically homogeneous city districts.

Since the behavior of these systems is not linear and predictable but inherently unpredictable, they are called complex systems. The only way to explore the behavior of these systems is to simulate them.

4.1 Simulation Concept

I begin by explaining how the urban system can be represented computationally. To this end, various forms of representation for space, time, and actors are introduced. Based on the paradigm of object-oriented programming (OOP), there will be a class for each of the following:

· Spatial elements such as streets, parcels, and buildings[14], which are treated as spatially fixed objects whose states (properties), however, change at certain points in time. In a first step of abstraction, these elements are transferred into the cells of a regular grid and stored by means of the state of such a cell. This structure forms the basis for the operation of a cellular automaton (CA). In a CA, the state and properties of a cell can be made dependent on the states of its neighboring cells and can change at every time step[15].

· Actors, whose entities are referred to below as agents. These can represent both individual and collective urban actors[16] . In contrast to cells, agents are mobile and can move freely across the cell grid (cellular space). Various kinds of communication among the agents, as well as with the cells, can be defined by means of the object methods (internal processing rules of the objects). The entire system of agents is called a multi-agent system (MAS)[17]. A system consisting of the two components CA and MAS forms an 'Inter Representation Network' (IRN)[18].

A simple example of an IRN is the 'path system' model (see prototype Fig. 01), in which the agents of the MAS move freely across the cellular space, marking the cells they have crossed. If an agent encounters a marked cell in its immediate surroundings, it tends to move in that direction, thereby reinforcing the existing marking. The system can be compared to footprints across a freshly snow­covered square, which over time are reinforced by other pedestrians or, if unused, are blown away again.

To represent the passage of time , the intention is to work with two time coordinates assigned to every object in the system, in order to distinguish events according to present, future, and past. This is necessary in order to take into account, for example, the effects of a future plan in relation to a current development, or overlaps with other plans.

Furthermore, the different speeds and temporal rhythms of the components must be taken into account: transportation systems and land uses change only over very long periods (centuries), the housing stock and the labor market are subject to a medium-fast rate of change (decades), whereas employment structure and population are subject to a fast rate of change (years). The transport of goods and passenger traffic take place immediately, whereas effects on the environment, such as air and noise pollution, occur indirectly[19]. For this purpose, internal clocks controlling the speeds can be assigned to the specific objects by means of their methods. The rhythms of change can be implemented via threshold values: an object stores marginal demands for change in a potential parameter, and a change takes place only when the potential exceeds the threshold value.

GIS serve as the data basis for the simulation models; their databases are accessed via 'loose coupling'[20], or specific GIS functions are integrated into the simulation environment, allowing direct data exchange[21]. The choice of method will only emerge in the course of the project from the possible planning applications.

4.2 Distribution of Population

An answer to the questions of why certain actors settle where they do and which activity spaces they claim for themselves depends on a multitude of influencing factors. Among these, particularly in urban space, is the land market, which is discussed under the next point. Land prices and densities of use are closely linked; they are, so to speak, two sides of the same coin (a change in one area does not take place without effects on the other): together, the two subsystems form a circular causality. Under this point, we will consider how centers come to be formed. Their effects are to be examined under point 4.3 Land Market.

The meaning of the term center can vary depending on the level of observation. Across the whole world, for example, commercial or technology centers are distributed in the form of major cities or regions. If one narrows the field of view to a country, cities are ranked according to their population or economic output. A city in itself in turn contains at least one city center, the so-called central business district (CBD). Individual urban areas differ according to whether they predominantly accommodate production, commercial, or residential uses, or, with a heterogeneous composition, count as mixed-use areas. The various areas form subordinate centers within the city, which define the type and density of development. This hierarchy of centers continues down into the dwellings, in which the rooms with the longest duration of use represent the central spaces.

The emergence and dynamics of the centers within a city discussed here depend on exogenous as well as endogenous influences. Exogenous influences are, for example, topographical conditions or urban planning concepts. The endogenous factors underlying the process of center formation consist of the preferences of individual or collective actors, which can be expressed economically by the value of a location and can be modeled as an "attracting" or "repelling" interaction between the different types of development (see segregation model, prototype Fig. 2). The value of a location depends on its distance to other locations (to be determined via accessibility analyses[22]) and on the social environment. These distances are evaluated in two ways: first, according to the travel costs saved or incurred by the choice of location (see economies of scale, prototype Fig. 3), and second, according to whether the view is pleasant, the surroundings suitable, and the sources of emissions, disturbances, and nuisances far away. The evaluation of relationships of the latter kind derives not from the prices of scarce resources but from the rates of spatial discounting[23].

Segregation model (see Fig. 2): Different agents (points marked blue and yellow in Fig. 2) represent uses that should not be located next to each other. In the model, the cells around an agent are marked according to its use. This space is, for example, impaired by the emissions of a commercial business (blue). Residential uses (yellow) stay away from these areas. Clusters of the different colors automatically form around the attachment points (red).

Economies of scale (see Fig. 3): The model shows how positive economies of scale affect the catchment area of a producer/retailer (market): certain costs arise in the manufacture of a product. If a larger number of products can be sold (catchment areas in different colors), the cost per product falls (economy of scale). It is therefore worthwhile for a buyer to travel a longer distance to acquire the more cheaply traded product, although this increases his travel costs. The increased demand in one market in turn leads to a further price reduction. In the resulting competition for sales areas, some suppliers can prevail and form local monopolies. At the boundaries of the catchment areas, travel costs and the cost of the product at the nearest market balance out. With more expensive products, this effect of economies of scale is intensified.

Environmental influences (resources, emissions, and immissions) are incorporated into the grid model as environmental data by means of the object properties of the cells; the model contains at least the components air pollution, noise pollution, consumption of natural resources, environmental and landscape qualities, and undeveloped space.

4.3 Land Market

Once the system of centers has been roughly defined, the boundary conditions for a land market model following Thünen (see Fig. 4) and Alonso have also been established. At the citywide (macro) level, this model governs the layout of plots and access routes. Furthermore, land prices establish the relationship between travel costs and densities of use (see point 4.2).

As a first approach to a solution, a bargaining model for land use following von Thünen is presented here (see prototype Fig. 4). In contrast to calculating ideal land zonings, here the ideal distribution of a given set of uses is negotiated.

Bargaining model (see Fig. 4): In the model, a cell represents a farmer who tries to maximize the profit from his crop. The profit depends on productivity, distance to the market, and transport costs for the different goods. The bargaining rules are defined such that each farmer compares, within a defined neighborhood, whether he could achieve a higher profit with his crop on another plot. If this is the case, he tries to swap it. If competition arises for the use of a parcel, the farmer who would earn a lower profit with his product at that location than his competitor loses out. A first particularity of this 'bottom-up' approach is the dependence of the land-use structure on the neighborhood within which a comparison takes place. If this neighborhood is relatively small, an ideal distribution does not come about.

Building on such a decentralized bargaining and comparison model, one of the fundamental tasks of this project is to be tackled, namely to demonstrate the interplay with the submodels for population redistribution (4.1) and the transportation system (4.3), which allows the formation and effects of land prices to be examined in detail: the demand for central goods leads to increased traffic toward the center and results in demand for space for mobile and immobile uses, which is reflected in prices per square meter. This interplay can lead to an efficient market equilibrium[24], which balances spatial and temporal scarcity and reproduces the course of the density and land price gradients, whose statistical regularity can be demonstrated empirically. The relativity of spatial and temporal scarcity consists in the fact that, first, spatial distance is translated into travel time and, second, travel time is made dependent on the spaciousness of the transportation corridors. The space devoted to transportation is subtracted from the space for the immobile uses it connects. The more space is used for fast and smoothly flowing traffic, the scarcer the space becomes for those uses that seek proximity to the center because of the time savings and higher returns.

Finally, traffic burdens in the form of noise and air pollution constitute the emissions for the environmental model, and the density of settlement affects the resources of undeveloped landscape. As a technical basis, e.g., for calculating the dispersion of exhaust gases, I draw on the diffusion model[25] . As immissions, the burdens and nuisances feed back into the rates of spatial discounting, which closes a further feedback loop via the environmental model to the evaluation of locations.

4.4 Transportation

How the transportation submodel is to be integrated into the overall model was shown under the last point (4.3). In the following, it is explained, first, how the structure of transportation links can be captured computationally and, second, how the use of this structure can be expressed.

Fractal structure of the transportation system: As a further form of self-organization, the fractal geometry of serving and served spaces is treated[26]. Starting from the smallest architectural unit – the single room – the built structure presents itself as a sequence of served spatial units and serving surrounding space: the room is accessed from the corridor, the apartment from the stairwell, the stairwell from the plot entrance, the block from the local access street, the neighborhood from the through road, and so on.

The data of the transportation network of the region under study can be taken from a GIS as the basis for deriving the fractal graph described. This yields the geometric-spatial structure of the network, which provides the initial data for path lengths, traffic loads, maintenance costs, etc. From this, the topological properties of a weighted graph are derived, on the basis of which accessibility analyses using the connectivity of the graph as well as cost-benefit ratios can be calculated. The former are relevant for location analyses and for statements about the gradation of access rights to certain spaces, which are closely related to the social structure of a city. The latter, in conjunction with land-use data, close the circle of effects to the land market. This circular dependency is accompanied by effects of multiplying parameters, the investigation of which is one of the central subjects of this project.

Use of the transportation system: Analogous to the spatially fractal structure of the access system, a fractal time structure can be observed in its use: one walks around the room so and so many times before stepping into the corridor; one walks around the apartment so and so many times before leaving it; one makes so and so many trips back and forth within the neighborhood before visiting surrounding neighborhoods; one drives around one's own city so and so many times before visiting another, and so on. Taken together, these commuting movements form a hierarchy of, in turn, self-similar rhythms and are mostly typically stable processes. They return to their starting point and tend toward an equilibrium.

The sum of an actor's movements over a certain period can be represented as a 'trace', which is called a trajectory , whose spatial extent in turn forms the activity space of an actor. Trajectories are recorded for every actor object (agent): a property acting as a 'historical container' stores the spatial coordinates of the paths the actor has traveled together with the associated time coordinates. This makes it possible to retrieve and analyze trajectories and activity spaces for any period, which is important for the following point.

4.5 Changes

In a city there is no central planning body that solves the problem of matching supply and demand. Nevertheless, devastating fluctuations between scarcity and oversupply are avoided over years and decades. This mysterious self-regulation becomes all the more puzzling when one considers the multifaceted nature of large cities. Buyers, sellers, administration, streets, bridges, and buildings are subject to constant change, so that the coherence of a city miraculously consists of a continuous flow of people and structures. Like a standing wave in front of a rock in a fast-flowing stream, a city forms a pattern in time.

In the language of complexity theory, this image by John Holland is described as a strange attractor, a system at the edge of chaos that neither tends toward an equilibrium point (attractor) nor slides into irregular chaos, but oscillates in between (see Fig. 5).

To make the processes in a city tangible for my investigations, not only the movements of an actor but also the course of all possible processes are captured by means of trajectories, whose shapes can be represented as four-dimensional (three spatial coordinates describing the position plus a time coordinate) 'lines', 'tubes', or 'trees'. A vivid example of tube-like processes are vehicles, whose footprint in principle remains the same but fluctuates insofar as the traffic area they occupy varies with driving speed. Tree-like processes are those in whose sequence of states objects are assembled from parts and dissolved into parts again. The standard example of a tree-like process is the history of a parcel that has acquired its current shape through repeated merging and subdivision.

Activity patterns can be derived from the shape of the trajectories (daily, weekly, seasonal, and annual exchange processes), which permit statements about the frequency of use of spatial units. These activity patterns are referred to as rhythms[27].

The classification of social processes according to the degree of stability of their rhythms (stable, conservative, unstable, self-organizing) is suitable as a new and promising approach to describing the spatial effects of changing time structures. As a general assumption, it can be held that wherever spatially permanent structures exist, we are dealing with stable processes in the associated activity patterns. Cities are so permanent as spatial structures because they harbor activity patterns with extraordinarily stable rhythms.

4.6 Visualization

Besides simulating urban mechanisms, a central concern of the project is to represent them graphically. Only through a generally comprehensible visualization of the processes can those involved in the planning process become aware of the problem of the dynamic dependencies of mutually influencing variables. The importance of the traceability of a simulation has already been discussed under the model criterion of transparency[28]. This requirement is implemented through the hierarchical structure of the subsystems, whose modes of operation can be understood by means of individual submodels. The prototypes already produced can serve as examples of the graphical presentation of process sequences; they were conceived as stand-alone Windows programs and are technically based on the Windows application programming interface (Windows API).

In addition to representing the dynamics of spatial processes, the visualization of spatial processes includes the vector-based depiction of the urban structure. For this purpose, the topological relations arising from spatial relationships must constantly be accompanied by a geometric representation. The restrictions associated with the geometry of the spatial elements are fed back into the topological possibilities of organization[29]. The vector-based depiction made possible in this way is intended to allow precise representation and a connection to the data structure of existing GIS.

5. PLANNING

In the course of this project, a computer program is to be developed that allows the effects of alternative plans and strategies within the urban fabric to be investigated by means of clearly defined scenario models. At this point, what the program is intended to achieve is summarized once more in conclusion:

· The manipulation of influencing variables (control parameters) via a graphical user interface allows interactive intervention in the running processes.

· The individual subprograms can serve to extend the functionality of existing GIS, for example for visualizing traffic flows and mapping activity spaces.

· The simulation of the complex relationships in urban fields of action, which is to be understood not as an all-encompassing urban model but as a "thinking tool", enables targeted forecasts of urban scenarios.

· On the one hand, the program to be designed can be used as a planning instrument, since it allows a better understanding of the complex relationships between various factors influencing urban development and thus facilitates administrative and political decisions, which are incorporated into the simulation program as exogenous influences.

· On the other hand, administrative and political decisions can be better communicated to the public if the relationships on which the decisions are based can be visualized and thus more easily understood (see Fig. 6).

· Last but not least, the visualization of spatial processes opens up new possibilities for public participation in urban planning (e-democracy). For example, different interests can be expressed as control parameters. The respective simulation models could be made accessible to citizens, so that the effects of the positions of different interest groups would become immediately apparent to the individual (see Fig. 6).

\\ Spatial Processes \\ Cellular Automata

Fundamentals of Cellular Automata

A cellular automaton is a computer model that usually consists of a regular arrangement of identical cells. Each cell can assume certain states and interacts with a defined number of neighboring cells. The basic components of such a system, the cells and the rules for calculating the next state of a cell, are very simply structured, but in their interplay they can give rise to complex systems. Four characteristics are to be distinguished:

The first is the geometry of the cell arrangement. Usually a rectangular grid of identical squares is used. Three- or four-dimensional arrangements can also be constructed without difficulty, but they can no longer be visualized so easily.

Second, it must be specified which positions in a given arrangement count as neighbors of any given cell. Two frequently occurring neighborhoods are shown in Fig. 01. In the von Neumann

Fig. 01. Left: von Neumann and

right: Moore neighborhood

neighborhood, the four directly adjacent cells above, below, to the left, and to the right are considered. If the four diagonally adjacent cells are counted in addition to these four, one speaks of the Moore neighborhood, in honor of Edward F. Moore.

The third parameter of a cellular automaton is the number of states per cell.

The fourth and last characteristic, which above all others accounts for the diversity in the universe of cellular automata, is the rule by which the future state of a cell is determined from the current constellation of its neighborhood (transition rule).

Cellular automata have numerous applications in architecture, urban design, and geography. In the following presentations, we concentrate on the urban context. Here we will examine in particular growth and traffic simulations, economic behavior, and the dynamics of processes of change. Once the underlying principles have been demonstrated, it becomes possible to generate urban structures that meet certain specifications.

Algorithms

In the cellular automaton considered below, for each cell in column X and row Y of the grid, the states (e.g., 0 or 1) of the Moore neighborhood (excluding the cell [X, Y] itself) are checked and the result is stored in a buffer (limboWorld).

for I := -1 to 1 do

begin

  for K := -1 to 1 do

  begin

    summe := summe + Zelle[X+K, Y+I].status;

  end;

end;

limboWorld[X, I] := summe - Zelle[X, Y].status;

Then, on the basis of the transition rule (limboWorld[X, I] >= 1), the respective status values of the cells are set to 0 or 1:

for I := -1 to 1 do

begin

  for K := -1 to 1 do

  begin

    If limboWorld[X, I] >= 1 Then

    begin

      Zelle[X, Y].status := 1;

    end else begin

      Zelle[X, Y].status := 0;

    end;

  end;

end;

By buffering in the limboWorld, we create a so-called pseudo-parallel procedure. The sequential processing of the neighborhood check in the first pass does not change the status values of the cells but merely stores the sums of the neighbors' status values. On the basis of these sums, the second loop uses the transition rule to decide which state the cells will assume in the next time step.

Formal Conventions

The formal notation of the algorithm given above is defined as follows:

The individual cells are denoted by the consecutive index i {i, i = 1,2,3, …, N}. N indicates the total number of cells in the system. Alternatively, for an exact position, the cells can also be noted with their x and y coordinates. The property Di(t)  of a cell indicates for a time step (t) whether the cell is developed(developed) Di(t) = 1 or not Di(t) = 0. In other contexts, one often speaks of alive/dead, on/off, or the like. The total development at a given time t, N(t), is determined by summing the development indices: . The neighborhood around a cell i is defined by , where the number of cells in each neighborhood is given by K and the sum of development in each neighborhood at time t correspondingly by . The number of states a cell can assume is defined by D . In the present example, D = 2 for developed and undeveloped.

Now the algorithm presented above can be expressed formally. The counting rule is based on a Moore neighborhood around the cell i under consideration. The Transition Rule is then represented as follows:

Programming Environment

For programming the simulations presented here, we used the language Delphi (formerly Object Pascal) and Borland's integrated development environment (IDE) of the same name. For newcomers to the field of simulating parallel processes, we recommend Netlogo. It provides both ready-made elements such as agents (turtles) and a cell structure, which can be accessed by means of simple commands. Other simulation environments include Processing, Repast, Swarm, Brahms and VBA (e.g., for AutoCAD).

Recommended Reading

For the introduction to the simulation concepts, we drew on the books 'Cities and Complexity’ by Michael Batty and 'Geosimulation’ by Itzhak Benenson and Paul M. Torrens, from which some ideas for the examples were adopted. For a more in-depth introduction to cellular automata, we recommend researching on wikipedia.

The City of Agents and Automata

Contact: Reinhard König

The texts and programs compiled here are part of the exhibition "Die Stadt im Reagenzglas" [The City in the Test Tube] by Reinhard König and Christian Bauriedel, first shown at the zkg-fhm gallery in Munich in 2006.

By clicking on the program images, the individual Windows programs can be downloaded and run. In the right-hand column, short descriptions of the models are available as PDF files. The poster at the top right provides a general introduction to the topic of computer-simulated urban models.

If you were referred to this page via the link in a publication, the programs offer the opportunity to try out the simulation models described in the article and to explore for yourself how the simulations work.

Experimenting with the models makes them easier to understand!
